Better
BET-ur
adj., adv.
Old English betera, the comparative of gōd (good), from a root meaning to remedy or make good. Webster 1828: having good qualities in a greater degree than another; improved in health; more advantageous. In the Authorized Version better is the load-bearing word of the epistle to the Hebrews, where it is used thirteen times to argue that what Christ brought does not supplement the old covenant but supersedes it.

Biblical Definition

Better is a comparative, and comparatives are arguments. The writer to the Hebrews builds his entire case on this one word: Jesus is made a surety of a better testament (Hebrews 7:22); He is the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises (Hebrews 8:6); the patriarchs desire a better country, that is, an heavenly (Hebrews 11:16). The Greek behind it, kreittōn, means stronger, more excellent, of higher rank — not merely more pleasant. That distinction is the whole argument. The old covenant was not bad; it was God-given, holy, just and good. It was simply weaker, because it ran through dying priests, repeated blood, and a copy of a sanctuary. What is better is better in the way a substance is better than its shadow. The word is not confined to Hebrews. David measures a single day against a thousand: a day in thy courts is better than a thousand (Psalm 84:10). Paul weighs his own death against continued usefulness and finds to be with Christ; which is far better (Philippians 1:23). In every case the comparison is not sentimental preference. It is a valuation, and the believer is expected to make it soberly and then act on it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BETTER as having good qualities in a greater degree than another; superior in excellence, worth, usefulness or acceptableness; improved in health; more advantageous. Webster notes it is the comparative of good, supplied from a different root.

expand to see more

BETTER, a. [comparative of good, supplied from a different root.] — Having good qualities in a greater degree than another; superior in excellence, worth, usefulness or acceptableness. Improved in health; less sick than before. More advantageous.

Webster’s phrase superior in excellence, worth, usefulness is precisely the register of Hebrews. The letter never says the old covenant was worthless; it says the new one is of higher worth. A comparison is only meaningful when both terms are real, which is why the argument requires the reader to honour Moses before he can measure Christ against him.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 7:22 — "By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament."

Hebrews 8:6 — "But now hath he obtained a more excellent ministry, by how much also he is the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises."

Hebrews 11:16 — "But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city."

Psalm 84:10 — "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness."

Philippians 1:23 — "For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better:"

Modern Corruption

Better is corrupted when the comparative of Hebrews is flattened into a claim that the old covenant was defective or sub-Christian, and equally when it is softened into mere preference — two errors that between them dissolve either the unity of Scripture or the finality of Christ.

expand to see more

The older error runs toward Marcion and never entirely dies: if the new covenant is better, the old must have been bad, its God harsher, its law an obstacle. Hebrews forbids this. The law was given by God, the tabernacle was patterned by God, the priesthood was appointed by God, and the writer treats every one of them with reverence. His argument is that a shadow is genuinely cast by a genuine body. What made the first covenant weak was not its author but its instruments — priests who died, blood that could not cleanse the conscience, a sanctuary made with hands. The Reformed reading holds both covenants as administrations of one covenant of grace, and it is precisely that unity which makes better intelligible rather than insulting.

The modern error is smaller and more common: better becomes a word of taste. Philippians 1:23 gets read as Paul expressing a personal preference for heaven, and Psalm 84:10 as poetic enthusiasm for church attendance. But Paul is doing arithmetic under the shadow of a possible execution, and David is stating a ratio — one day against a thousand, a doorkeeper’s post against the tents of wickedness. Scripture’s comparatives are valuations a man is expected to act upon. When better means only what I happen to like more, the entire logic of counting the cost collapses, and with it the possibility of martyrdom, which is simply this word taken seriously.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Authorized Version’s better renders a Greek comparative of strength and rank in Hebrews, and the ordinary Hebrew word for good in comparative constructions in the Old Testament. The difference matters: the Hebrew compares goods, the Greek compares ranks.

expand to see more

Greek kreittōn — stronger, more excellent, of higher rank; the structural word of Hebrews (7:22; 8:6; 11:16). Untagged in this lexicon; no Strong’s page is minted for it here.

Hebrew tōv (H2896) — good, pleasant, beneficial; rendered better in comparative constructions (Psalm 84:10, better than a thousand).

Greek hyperechō (G5242) — to surpass, to excel, to be superior; the cousin idea behind a more excellent ministry (Hebrews 8:6).

Greek para (G3844) — beside, alongside; the preposition Hebrews uses to set the two covenants side by side so the comparison can be made at all.

Usage

"Hebrews argues by comparative: a better testament, a better covenant, better promises, a better country — superiority of rank, not a correction of a mistake."

"A day in thy courts is better than a thousand (Psalm 84:10) is a ratio, not a compliment."

"To be with Christ; which is far better (Philippians 1:23) — Paul weighs death against usefulness and reports the sum."
